notes.definition: Substances made of small molecules are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting and boiling points, because only the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules are overcome when they melt or boil, not the strong covalent bonds.
explanation: Substances that consist of small molecules, such as water (H₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), oxygen (O₂) and chlorine (Cl₂), are usually gases or liquids at room temperature. They have relatively low melting points and boiling points. Inside each molecule the atoms are held together by strong covalent bonds. Between the molecules there are only weak forces of attraction, called intermolecular forces.

When a substance made of small molecules melts or boils, it is these weak intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds. The molecules separate from each other but each molecule stays intact. For example, when water boils, the H₂O molecules move apart to form steam, but the O–H bonds inside each molecule do not break. Because the intermolecular forces are weak, only a small amount of energy is needed to overcome them, which is why the melting and boiling points are low.

The intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points. For example, in the alkanes, methane (CH₄) boils at −162 °C, propane (C₃H₈) at −42 °C and hexane (C₆H₁₄) at 69 °C. The halogens show the same pattern: fluorine and chlorine are gases at room temperature, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. Larger molecules have stronger forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate them.

Substances made of small molecules do not conduct electricity, because the molecules do not have an overall electric charge. There are no ions and no delocalised electrons that can move and carry charge. This is true whether the substance is solid, liquid or gas. Pure water, for example, is a very poor conductor; tap water conducts slightly only because it contains dissolved ions.

You should be able to use the idea that intermolecular forces are weak compared with covalent bonds to explain the bulk properties of molecular substances. A useful way to remember it: strong covalent bonds decide what the molecule is; weak intermolecular forces decide whether the substance is a solid, liquid or gas. Do not confuse substances made of small molecules with giant covalent structures such as diamond, where melting requires many strong covalent bonds to be broken.
keyFacts: Small molecular substances are usually gases or liquids at room temperature.
They have relatively low melting points and boiling points.
Covalent bonds within the molecules are strong.
Intermolecular forces between the molecules are weak.
On melting or boiling, the intermolecular forces are overcome, not the covalent bonds.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
Small molecular substances do not conduct electricity: the molecules have no overall charge.
Examples: H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃, HCl.

keyTerms.definition: A particle made of a small, fixed number of atoms joined by covalent bonds, such as H₂O or CO₂.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules.
A strong bond formed by a shared pair of electrons between two atoms within a molecule.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas; for small molecules it is low because intermolecular forces are weak.
Properties of a substance as a whole, such as melting point and conductivity, which depend on the forces between many particles.
The net charge on a particle; molecules have no overall charge, so they cannot carry a current.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a low boiling point
workedExamples.question: Explain why methane, CH₄, has a low boiling point (−162 °C).
steps: Methane is made of small molecules.
There are only weak intermolecular forces between the molecules.
When methane boils, these weak forces are overcome; the covalent C–H bonds do not break.
Only a small amount of energy is needed, so the boiling point is low.
workedExamples.answer: Weak intermolecular forces between small molecules need little energy to overcome.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a trend in boiling points
workedExamples.question: Explain why pentane (C₅H₁₂, boiling point 36 °C) has a higher boiling point than propane (C₃H₈, boiling point −42 °C).
steps: Both are made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces.
Pentane molecules are larger than propane molecules.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules.
More energy is needed to overcome the stronger intermolecular forces in pentane.
workedExamples.answer: Pentane's larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.

workedExamples.title: Predicting state from boiling point data
workedExamples.question: Butane boils at −1 °C and hexane boils at 69 °C. Calculate the difference in boiling points and give the state of each at 25 °C. (Both melt below −90 °C.)
steps: At 25 °C butane is above its boiling point, so it is a gas.
At 25 °C hexane is between its melting point and boiling point, so it is a liquid.
workedExamples.answer: 70 °C difference; butane is a gas and hexane is a liquid at 25 °C.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say that covalent bonds break when water boils.
misconceptions.right: Only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome. Steam is still made of H₂O molecules.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say small molecules have low boiling points because covalent bonds are weak.
misconceptions.right: Covalent bonds are strong. The boiling point is low because the intermolecular forces are weak.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think water conducts electricity because it is a liquid.
misconceptions.right: Pure water is made of molecules with no overall charge, so it is a very poor conductor. Tap water conducts slightly because it has dissolved ions.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse intermolecular forces with intramolecular (covalent) bonds.
misconceptions.right: Inter means between molecules (weak); the covalent bonds are inside molecules (strong).

realWorld: Liquefied petroleum gas (propane and butane) is easily turned into a liquid under pressure because the intermolecular forces are weak.
Fractional distillation separates crude oil using the different boiling points of molecules of different sizes.
Dry ice (solid CO₂) turns straight into a gas at −78 °C because the forces between CO₂ molecules are weak.
examTips: Always write 'weak intermolecular forces' (or 'weak forces between molecules'). Writing 'weak bonds' or 'weak covalent bonds' loses marks.
State clearly that the covalent bonds are NOT broken when a small molecular substance melts or boils.
For trends, link: larger molecules → stronger intermolecular forces → more energy needed → higher boiling point.
For conductivity, say 'molecules have no overall charge' (no ions or delocalised electrons to carry charge).
summary: Small molecules are usually gases or liquids with low melting and boiling points.
Strong covalent bonds inside molecules; weak intermolecular forces between them.
Melting and boiling overcome the intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds.
Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and higher melting and boiling points.
Small molecular substances do not conduct electricity: molecules have no overall charge.

flashcards.front: What is overcome when a small molecular substance boils?
flashcards.back: The weak intermolecular forces (not the covalent bonds).

How does molecule size affect intermolecular forces?

questions.question: What is the usual state at room temperature of a substance made of small molecules?
markScheme: 1 mark: Gas or liquid
questions.explanation: Small molecular substances usually have low melting and boiling points, so they are gases or liquids at room temperature.

questions.question: What is overcome when water boils?
options: Covalent bonds between O and H atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: Weak intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: Boiling separates whole H₂O molecules; the O–H covalent bonds stay intact.

questions.question: Why does chlorine not conduct electricity?
options: Its molecules have no overall electric charge.
It contains ions that cannot move.
markScheme: 1 mark: Its molecules have no overall electric charge.
questions.explanation: Cl₂ molecules have no overall charge, and there are no ions or delocalised electrons to carry current.

questions.question: Which substance consists of small molecules and has a low boiling point?
markScheme: 1 mark: Carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: CO₂ is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces. Sodium chloride is ionic, diamond is giant covalent and copper is metallic.

questions.question: Which statement about the forces in a substance made of small molecules is correct?
options: Covalent bonds and intermolecular forces are both weak.
Covalent bonds are strong; intermolecular forces are weak.
Covalent bonds are weak; intermolecular forces are strong.
There are no forces between molecules.
markScheme: 1 mark: Covalent bonds are strong; intermolecular forces are weak.
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds within molecules are strong; the forces between molecules are weak.

questions.question: Which alkane has the highest boiling point?
markScheme: 1 mark: C₅H₁₂
questions.explanation: C₅H₁₂ (pentane) is the largest molecule, so it has the strongest intermolecular forces and the highest boiling point.

questions.question: Bromine (Br₂) is a liquid at room temperature but chlorine (Cl₂) is a gas. Why?
options: Br₂ molecules are larger, so the intermolecular forces are stronger.
markScheme: 1 mark: Br₂ molecules are larger, so the intermolecular forces are stronger.
questions.explanation: Bromine molecules are larger than chlorine molecules, giving stronger intermolecular forces and a higher boiling point.

questions.question: Substance Y melts at −95 °C, boils at 56 °C and does not conduct electricity in any state. What is the structure of Y?
markScheme: 1 mark: Small molecules
questions.explanation: Low melting and boiling points with no conductivity indicate small molecules held by weak intermolecular forces.

questions.question: A student writes: 'When ice melts, the covalent bonds in water break, so it needs only a little energy because covalent bonds are weak.' How many scientific errors are in this statement?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2
questions.explanation: Two errors: covalent bonds do not break on melting (intermolecular forces are overcome), and covalent bonds are strong, not weak.

questions.question: Sulfur exists as S₈ molecules and melts at 115 °C. Oxygen exists as O₂ molecules and melts at −218 °C. What best explains the difference?
options: S₈ molecules are much larger, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger.
The covalent bonds in S₈ are broken when it melts.
markScheme: 1 mark: S₈ molecules are much larger, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger.
questions.explanation: Both are molecular. S₈ molecules are much larger than O₂ molecules, so the forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to melt sulfur.

questions.question: Butane boils at −1 °C and pentane boils at 36 °C. Calculate the difference in their boiling points.
Methane boils at −162 °C and propane boils at −42 °C. Calculate the difference in their boiling points.
questions.explanation: −42 + 162 = 120 °C. Propane's larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.

questions.question: The boiling points of three alkanes are −89 °C, −42 °C and −1 °C. Calculate the mean boiling point. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

The boiling points of the halogens are: fluorine −188 °C, chlorine −34 °C, bromine 59 °C, iodine 184 °C. Calculate the mean increase in boiling point from one halogen to the next, from fluorine to iodine.
markScheme: 1 mark: total increase = 184 − (−188) = 372 °C
1 mark: 372 ÷ 3 steps = 124 °C
questions.explanation: There are three steps (F→Cl, Cl→Br, Br→I). Total increase 372 °C ÷ 3 = 124 °C. Check: 154 + 93 + 125 = 372.

questions.question: Give two properties of substances made of small molecules.
acceptedAnswers: gas or liquid at room temperature
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: low melting point; low boiling point; usually gases or liquids at room temperature; do not conduct electricity
questions.explanation: These follow from weak intermolecular forces and uncharged molecules.

questions.question: State what is meant by intermolecular forces.
markScheme: 1 mark: (weak) forces of attraction between molecules
questions.explanation: Inter means between: these forces act between separate molecules.

questions.question: Explain why oxygen, O₂, has a very low boiling point (−183 °C).
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen consists of small molecules
1 mark: (only) weak intermolecular forces between molecules
1 mark: little energy needed to overcome them (covalent bonds are not broken)
questions.explanation: The three marks come from structure, the weak forces and the energy needed.

questions.question: Explain why ammonia, NH₃, does not conduct electricity.
markScheme: 1 mark: ammonia is made of (small) molecules
1 mark: which have no overall electric charge (no ions or free electrons to carry charge)
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charged particles; neutral molecules cannot carry a current.

questions.question: Describe what happens to the particles when liquid chlorine boils.
markScheme: 1 mark: intermolecular forces are overcome / molecules move apart
1 mark: the Cl₂ molecules stay intact / covalent bonds do not break
questions.explanation: Chlorine gas is still made of Cl₂ molecules; only the forces between them have been overcome.

questions.question: Describe the trend in boiling points of the alkanes as the molecules get larger, and explain it.
markScheme: 1 mark: boiling point increases as molecules get larger
1 mark: because intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules (more energy needed)
questions.explanation: The spec states that intermolecular forces increase with size, giving higher melting and boiling points.

questions.question: Iodine, I₂, is a solid at room temperature but fluorine, F₂, is a gas. Both consist of small molecules. Explain the difference.
markScheme: 1 mark: iodine molecules are larger than fluorine molecules
1 mark: so the intermolecular forces are stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them (higher melting/boiling point)
questions.explanation: The halogens show how molecule size affects the strength of intermolecular forces.

questions.question: Hydrogen chloride gas, HCl, does not conduct electricity, but hydrochloric acid (HCl dissolved in water) does. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: HCl gas is made of molecules with no overall charge
1 mark: in water HCl forms ions (H⁺ and Cl⁻) that are free to move and carry charge
questions.explanation: Hydrogen chloride reacts with water to form ions, so the solution contains mobile charged particles even though the gas does not.

questions.question: Which pair of substances are both made of small molecules?
markScheme: 1 mark: H₂O and CH₄
questions.explanation: Water and methane are both small covalent molecules. NaCl is ionic, SiO₂ is giant covalent and Cu is a metal.

questions.question: State whether intermolecular forces are stronger or weaker than covalent bonds.
markScheme: 1 mark: (much) weaker
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces are weak compared with covalent bonds, which is why small molecular substances melt and boil easily without the molecules breaking apart.

questions.question: Hexane, C₆H₁₄, boils at 69 °C. Predict whether octane, C₈H₁₈, has a higher or lower boiling point than hexane. Give a reason.
markScheme: 1 mark: higher
1 mark: octane molecules are larger, so the intermolecular forces are stronger (more energy needed to overcome them)
questions.explanation: Octane's boiling point is about 126 °C. Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.

questions.question: Explain why substances made of small molecules have low melting points and do not conduct electricity. Use water as an example.
markScheme: Indicative content: water is made of small H₂O molecules; strong covalent bonds within each molecule; weak intermolecular forces between molecules; when ice melts / water boils, only intermolecular forces are overcome; covalent bonds not broken; little energy needed, so low melting and boiling points; molecules have no overall electric charge; no ions or delocalised electrons; so pure water does not conduct electricity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation of both the low melting point and the lack of conductivity, distinguishing intermolecular forces from covalent bonds
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct points, for example 'weak forces' or 'no charge', with limited explanation
questions.explanation: Good answers are precise: weak intermolecular forces (not weak bonds) explain the low melting point; uncharged molecules explain the lack of conductivity.

questions.question:
The table shows data for four substances.
Substance A: melting point 801 °C, boiling point 1413 °C, conducts when molten.
Substance B: melting point −182 °C, boiling point −162 °C, does not conduct.
Substance C: melting point −7 °C, boiling point 59 °C, does not conduct.
Substance D: melting point 114 °C, boiling point 184 °C, does not conduct.
Identify which substances consist of small molecules. Explain your choice and explain the differences in boiling point between these substances.
markScheme: Indicative content: B, C and D are small molecules; low melting and boiling points compared with A; do not conduct in any state, so no ions or delocalised electrons, molecules have no overall charge; A is ionic (high melting point, conducts when molten). Boiling points: B < C < D; weak intermolecular forces overcome on boiling, not covalent bonds; intermolecular forces increase with size of molecules; so D has the largest molecules and strongest intermolecular forces, B the smallest; more energy needed to overcome stronger forces; B gas, C liquid, D solid at room temperature.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): B, C and D correctly identified with reasons; a clear explanation of the boiling point order in terms of molecular size and intermolecular forces; covalent bonds stated not to break
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): small molecular substances mostly identified with some reasoning, and a basic link between intermolecular forces and boiling point
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two correct identifications or simple statements about low boiling points
questions.explanation: B is methane, C is bromine and D is iodine; A is sodium chloride. The key is that low melting point plus no conductivity means small molecules, and boiling point rises with molecular size.
